herodotus.name: Herodotus
herodotus.summary: Greek historian and geographer (c. 484–c. 425 BC), called 'the Father of History' for his Histories, a detailed account of the Greco-Persian Wars and the peoples and lands around them.

histories-herodotus.name: Histories
histories-herodotus.summary: Herodotus's work from the 5th century BC, considered the founding text of history writing in the West, covering the rise of the Persian Empire and the Greco-Persian Wars.

scythians.name: Scythians
scythians.summary: An ancient Eastern Iranic nomadic people who migrated from Central Asia to the Pontic Steppe in the 9th-8th centuries BC, dominating the region through mounted warfare before being conquered by the Sarmatians in the 3rd-2nd centuries BC.

kumis.name: Kumis
kumis.summary: Traditional fermented drink made from mare's milk, central to Turkic and Mongolic peoples of the Central and East Asian steppes, also called airag, with a higher alcohol content than kefir.

fractional-freezing.name: Freeze distillation
fractional-freezing.summary: A process of separating substances by partial freezing, historically used to concentrate alcohol in drinks such as fermented mare's milk.

animal-style.name: Animal style
animal-style.summary: A decorative art style emphasizing animal motifs, made by herding peoples from the Ordos region to Northern Europe from the early Iron Age through the Migration Period.

scytho-siberian-art.name: Scytho-Siberian art
scytho-siberian-art.summary: Decorative art, especially jewellery, of nomadic Eurasian Steppe peoples from about the 7th to 3rd centuries BC, including the distinctive Animal Style depicting real and fantastical creatures.

greco-buddhist-art.name: Greco-Buddhist art
greco-buddhist-art.summary: Also called Gandhara art, a style blending Ancient Greek and Buddhist art that flowered under the Kushan Empire and produced the first known depictions of the Buddha in human form.

serindian-art.name: Serindian art
serindian-art.summary: Art that developed from the 2nd to 11th century CE in Serindia (Xinjiang), blending Greco-Buddhist styles from Gandhara with Chinese and Persian influences via the Silk Road.

greco-bactrian-kingdom.name: Greco-Bactrian Kingdom
greco-bactrian-kingdom.summary: A Hellenistic Greek kingdom in Central Asia and Afghanistan, founded around 256 BC by Diodotus I Soter, that dominated the region until its fall around 120 BC.

ai-khanoum.name: Ai-Khanoum
ai-khanoum.summary: Ruins of a Hellenistic Greek city in northern Afghanistan, founded around 300–285 BCE under the Seleucid dynasty, that later served the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom until its destruction around 145 BCE.

indo-greek-kingdom.name: Indo-Greek Kingdom
indo-greek-kingdom.summary: Hellenistic-era Greek kingdoms ruling parts of northwestern South Asia from about 200 BCE, founded after a Bactrian Greek king invaded India; they blended Greek and Indian art, language and religion.

kushan-empire.name: Kushan Empire
kushan-empire.summary: A syncretic empire (c. 30–375 CE) formed by the Yuezhi, spreading from Bactria across what is now Afghanistan, Pakistan and northern India; its rulers patronized Buddhism and helped spread it into Central Asia and China.

gandhara.name: Gandhara
gandhara.summary: An ancient Indo-Aryan region centered on the Peshawar valley, in what is now northwest Pakistan and northeast Afghanistan, known as an influential Buddhist civilization.

tarim-basin.name: Tarim Basin
tarim-basin.summary: A large endorheic basin in Xinjiang, northwestern China, dominated by the Taklamakan Desert and historically called Altishahr.

eucratides-i.name: Eucratides I
eucratides-i.summary: One of the most important Greco-Bactrian kings, reigning 172/171–145 BC, who conquered large parts of northern India and minted extensive coinage; his successors were the last Greek kings in Bactria.

dunhuang.name: Dunhuang
dunhuang.summary: Oasis city in northwestern China and major Silk Road stop, known for the nearby Mogao Caves and its position at the entrance to the Hexi Corridor.

zhang-qian.name: Zhang Qian
zhang-qian.summary: Chinese diplomat and explorer (died c. 114 BC) sent by Emperor Wu of Han into Central Asia, whose travels opened the Silk Road between East and West.

bactria.name: Bactria
bactria.summary: An ancient Iranian region of Central Asia between the Oxus River and the Hindu Kush, an early centre of Zoroastrianism later ruled by the Achaemenid Empire and conquered by Alexander the Great.

emperor-wu-of-han.name: Emperor Wu of Han
emperor-wu-of-han.summary: Seventh emperor of the Han dynasty, reigning from 141 to 87 BCE for 54 years, a record among Han emperors. His rule brought vast territorial expansion, a centralized state, and increased contact with western Eurasia.

xiongnu.name: Xiongnu
xiongnu.summary: A nomadic tribal confederation dominating the eastern Eurasian steppe from the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD, founded as an empire by Modu Chanyu, eventually defeated by the Han dynasty.

alexander-the-great.name: Alexander the Great
alexander-the-great.summary: King of Macedon from 336 BC who conquered much of the known world by age 30, creating an empire stretching from Greece to India; tutored by Aristotle.

alexandria-eschate.name: Alexandria Eschate
alexandria-eschate.summary: A city founded by Alexander the Great in 329 BC at the edge of Central Asia, near modern Khujand, Tajikistan; his empire's most northerly outpost.

first-turkic-khaganate.name: First Turkic Khaganate
first-turkic-khaganate.summary: A Turkic empire founded around 552 CE by the Ashina clan of the Göktürks, stretching from Manchuria to the Black Sea before splitting into eastern and western halves in 603.

median-kingdom.name: Median Empire
median-kingdom.summary: A polity centered on Ecbatana from the 7th to mid-6th century BCE that, allied with Babylonia, helped overthrow the Neo-Assyrian Empire and expanded under Cyaxares to form what is called the first Iranian empire.

achaemenid-empire.name: Achaemenid Empire
achaemenid-empire.summary: Ancient Iranian empire founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BC, the largest of its time, stretching from the Balkans to the Indus Valley before Alexander the Great conquered it in 330 BC.

huns.name: Huns
huns.summary: A nomadic people from Central Asia who built a short-lived empire on Rome's Danube frontier by 430 CE, launching devastating raids under King Attila until his death in 453.

seleucid-empire.name: Seleucid Empire
seleucid-empire.summary: A Greek state in West Asia founded by Seleucus I Nicator in 312 BC after Alexander the Great's empire divided, ruling from Seleucia and Antioch until Rome annexed it in 63 BC.

wars-of-the-diadochi.name: Wars of the Diadochi
wars-of-the-diadochi.summary: The struggles among Alexander the Great's generals for control of his empire after his death in 323 BC, lasting until 272 BC and establishing the Ptolemaic and Seleucid dynasties.

bactrian-language.name: Bactrian language
bactrian-language.summary: An Eastern Iranian language once spoken in Bactria, used as the official language of the Kushan and Hephthalite empires.

saka.name: Saka
saka.summary: Nomadic Eastern Iranian peoples of the Eurasian Steppe and Tarim Basin from the 9th century BC to the 5th century AD, closely related to the Scythians.

yona.name: Yavanas (Yona)
yona.summary: Sanskrit and Pali term used in ancient India to designate Greek speakers, derived from 'Ionians,' appearing in the edicts of Ashoka and other ancient texts.

kambojas.name: Kambojas
kambojas.summary: A southeastern Iranian people who lived at the edge of Iranian-populated lands bordering India, first mentioned in later Vedic-period texts, and adherents of Zoroastrianism.

pahlavas.name: Pahlavas
pahlavas.summary: A people mentioned in ancient Indian texts such as the Puranas and Mahabharata, linked to the Saka-Parthians.

parada-kingdom.name: Paradas
parada-kingdom.summary: An Iron Age kingdom of uncertain location described in ancient Indian texts, variously placed in Central Asia, Xinjiang or the Himalayas, and thought linked to the later Paratarajas dynasty.

hotan.name: Hotan (Khotan)
hotan.summary: An oasis town in southwestern Xinjiang, China, on the southern Silk Road route through the Tarim Basin, historically dependent on the Karakash and White Jade rivers at the edge of the Taklamakan Desert.

mahayana.name: Mahayana
mahayana.summary: The largest branch of Buddhism, developed in India from around the 1st century BCE, distinguished by its own scriptures and its ideal of the bodhisattva who seeks buddhahood to save all beings.

puranas.name: Puranas
puranas.summary: A vast genre of Hindu and Jain literature covering legends, cosmology and genealogies of gods and kings, with the first versions likely composed between the 3rd and 10th centuries CE.

haihaya-kingdom.name: Haihaya kingdom
haihaya-kingdom.summary: A kingdom in the Mahabharata epic ruled by Yadava kings in central and western India, with its capital at Mahishmati, eventually destroyed by the warrior Parashurama.

al-biruni.name: Al-Biruni
al-biruni.summary: Iranian polymath of the Islamic Golden Age (c. 973-1050) who served the Ghaznavids as a historian and court astrologer and wrote a landmark work on India around 1030.

kharosthi.name: Kharosthi Script
kharosthi.summary: An ancient Indic writing system developed in the Gandhara region between the 5th and 3rd centuries BCE, used along the Silk Road until dying out around the 5th century CE.

endere.name: Endere
endere.summary: Archaeological site in the southern Taklamakan Desert of Xinjiang, China, on the ancient Silk Road's southern route, tentatively identified with a place called Saca.

ma-duanlin.name: Ma Duanlin
ma-duanlin.summary: Chinese historical writer and encyclopaedist, 1245 to 1322, who compiled the comprehensive encyclopedia Wenxian Tongkao during the Yuan dynasty.

issyk-kurgan.name: Issyk kurgan
issyk-kurgan.summary: A Saka burial mound in south-eastern Kazakhstan dated to the 4th or 3rd century BC, discovered in 1969, notable for a silver cup bearing an inscription.

pazyryk-culture.name: Pazyryk culture
pazyryk-culture.summary: An Iron Age nomadic Scythian culture of the 6th to 3rd centuries BCE, known from mummies and artifacts preserved in burial mounds in the Siberian permafrost of the Altai Mountains.

altai-mountains.name: Altai Mountains
altai-mountains.summary: Mountain range in Central Asia where Russia, China, Mongolia, and Kazakhstan meet, home to a sparse, ethnically diverse population including Turkic peoples and Mongols.

sogdia.name: Sogdia
sogdia.summary: An ancient Iranian civilisation between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, conquered in turn by Persian, Greek and other empires; its merchants were key middlemen on the Silk Road.

gastraphetes.name: Gastraphetes
gastraphetes.summary: A hand-held crossbow used by the ancient Greeks, described by Heron of Alexandria and considered a forerunner of the catapult, invented before around 420 BCE.

ulaanzuukh-culture.name: Ulaanzuukh culture
ulaanzuukh-culture.summary: A Late Bronze Age archaeological culture of eastern Mongolia, dated to about 1450–1000 BCE, likely ancestral to the later Slab-grave culture.

slab-grave-culture.name: Slab-grave culture
slab-grave-culture.summary: A Late Bronze Age to Early Iron Age archaeological culture of Mongolia, about 1300 to 300 BC, a major ancestral component of the later Xiongnu.

sarmatians.name: Sarmatians
sarmatians.summary: A confederation of nomadic Iranian horse peoples who dominated the Pontic steppe from about the 5th century BC to the 4th century AD, later clashing and allying with Rome and the Goths.

tashtyk-culture.name: Tashtyk culture
tashtyk-culture.summary: A Late Iron Age archaeological culture that flourished in Siberia's Yenisei valley from the 1st to 4th centuries CE, following the earlier Tagar culture.

oglakhty.name: Oglakhty
oglakhty.summary: A mountain range and Tashtyk-culture burial complex in Khakassia, Russia, dated to the 1st century BCE, whose dry soil preserved perishable materials such as wood, leather and fabric.

khakassia.name: Khakassia
khakassia.summary: A republic of Russia in southern Siberia, with its capital at Abakan, known for its rivers, mountains, and the Khakassky Nature Reserve.

chanyu.name: Chanyu
chanyu.summary: Title used for eight centuries by supreme rulers of Inner Asian nomads, most famously the Xiongnu, until replaced by "Khagan" in 402 AD.

kanishka.name: Kanishka
kanishka.summary: A Kushan emperor (r. c. 127–150 CE) whose empire stretched from Central Asia to the Gangetic plain, and whose patronage helped spread Buddhism along the Silk Road.

fergana-valley.name: Fergana Valley
fergana-valley.summary: Fertile Central Asian valley spanning parts of modern Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, a historic crossroads of Greek, Chinese, Bactrian and Parthian civilizations and homeland of Mughal founder Babur.

western-regions.name: Western Regions
western-regions.summary: A historical Chinese term for lands west of the Yumen Pass, mainly the Tarim Basin and Central Asia, strategically important along the Silk Road since at least the 3rd century BC.

wusun.name: Wusun
wusun.summary: Ancient semi-nomadic steppe people recorded in Chinese sources from the 2nd century BC, who settled the Ili Valley and became close allies of the Han dynasty for centuries.

kangju.name: Kangju
kangju.summary: A Central Asian kingdom of the early first millennium CE, likely linked to Sogdiana, ranked by Chinese sources as the second most powerful state in Transoxiana.

transoxiana.name: Transoxiana
transoxiana.summary: A Central Asian region beyond the Amu Darya river, named by Alexander the Great's troops in the 4th century BCE and later a Persian Achaemenid province called Sogdia.

khwarazm.name: Khwarazm
khwarazm.summary: A large oasis region on the Amu Darya river delta in Central Asia, center of the Iranian Khwarezmian civilization until Turkic tribes took over in the 9th century.

dayuan.name: Dayuan
dayuan.summary: The Chinese name for a kingdom in Central Asia's Ferghana Valley, described as descended from Greek settlers, with walled cities and a wine-making culture.

shaivism.name: Shaivism
shaivism.summary: A branch of Hindu tradition worshipping Shiva as the supreme being, rooted in Vedic worship of Rudra, which became dominant in several Hindu kingdoms and later spread into Southeast Asia.

modu-chanyu.name: Modu Chanyu
modu-chanyu.summary: Founder of the Xiongnu Empire, who seized power by having his father killed in 209 BCE, then unified Mongolian-Manchurian tribes into an empire stretching from the Liao River to the Pamir Mountains.

emperor-guangwu-of-han.name: Emperor Guangwu of Han
emperor-guangwu-of-han.summary: Founding emperor of China's Eastern Han dynasty (5 BC–AD 57), who reunified China by 36 CE after civil war and made Taoism the dynasty's official religion.

tanshihuai.name: Tanshihuai
tanshihuai.summary: Xianbei chieftain (137–181) during the late Eastern Han dynasty who unified the Xianbei into a polity that long threatened Han China's northern borders, though it collapsed after his death.

xianbei.name: Xianbei
xianbei.summary: A nomadic, multi-ethnic confederation on the eastern Eurasian steppe descended from the Donghu, who rose to dominate the Mongolian Plateau after replacing the Xiongnu.

protectorate-of-the-western-regions.name: Protectorate of the Western Regions
protectorate-of-the-western-regions.summary: A Han dynasty Chinese administration over the Tarim Basin region, existing on and off from 59/60 BCE to 439 CE, marking the first direct Chinese rule there.

karasahr.name: Karasahr
karasahr.summary: An ancient Silk Road town in Xinjiang, also known by the Chinese name Yanqi, near where the Han dynasty stationed its Protector General of the Western Regions.

book-of-the-later-han.name: Book of the Later Han
book-of-the-later-han.summary: One of China's Twenty-Four Histories, covering the Later Han dynasty from 6 to 189 CE and compiled by Fan Ye and others in the 5th century.

ban-chao.name: Ban Chao
ban-chao.summary: A Chinese diplomat, explorer and Han-dynasty general (32–102 CE) who governed Central Asia's Western Regions, fought the Xiongnu for over 30 years and restored Han control over the Tarim Basin.

yuezhi.name: Yuezhi
yuezhi.summary: An ancient nomadic people from Gansu whose defeat by the Xiongnu in 176 BC set off migrations that eventually produced the Kushan Empire.

tengrism.name: Tengrism
tengrism.summary: A belief system from the Eurasian steppes based on shamanism and animism and centered on the sky god Tengri, once the state religion of several medieval Turkic and Mongol states.

tengri.name: Tengri
tengri.summary: The sky god of traditional Turkic and Mongolic beliefs, seen as eternal, supreme, and the judge and source of life; worship centered on him is called Tengrism.

indo-iranians.name: Indo-Iranians
indo-iranians.summary: A group of Proto-Indo-European-speaking peoples who spread Indo-Iranian languages across Eurasia from the early 2nd millennium BCE, originating near modern Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan before splitting into Iranian and Indo-Aryan branches.

historical-vedic-religion.name: Historical Vedic religion
historical-vedic-religion.summary: The religious ideas and practices of Indo-Aryan peoples in northwest India during the Vedic period (c. 1500–500 BCE), recorded in Vedic texts and one of the major traditions that shaped modern Hinduism.

anahit.name: Anahit
anahit.summary: Goddess of fertility, healing, wisdom and water in Armenian mythology, originally a war goddess, who by the 5th century BCE became Armenia's main deity alongside Aramazd.

helios.name: Helios
helios.summary: The Greek god personifying the Sun, usually shown with a radiant crown driving a chariot across the sky; a minor deity in Classical Greece whose worship grew more prominent later.

yeniseian-peoples.name: Yeniseian peoples
yeniseian-peoples.summary: Modern or ancient Siberian populations speaking Yeniseian languages; today only the Ket and Yugh survive, numbering just over a thousand, likely descended from groups that migrated north from near Lake Baikal.

shamanism-in-siberia.name: Siberian shamanism
shamanism-in-siberia.summary: Shamanistic religious and cultural practices followed by many peoples across North Asia, particularly Siberia, which some researchers consider shamanism's heartland.

mithra.name: Mithra
mithra.summary: An ancient Iranian deity of covenants, light, oaths, justice, the sun and friendship, later linked to the Roman god Mithras through Zoroastrian influence.

ahura-mazda.name: Ahura Mazda
ahura-mazda.summary: The chief god and sky deity of Zoroastrianism, first prominently invoked in the Achaemenid-era Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great.

verethragna.name: Verethragna
verethragna.summary: A Zoroastrian yazata, or divine being, also known as Bahram.

siy-vash.name: Siyâvash
siy-vash.summary: A major figure in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, son of Shah Kay Kāvus, celebrated for his righteousness after proving his innocence in a trial by fire, though it strained his bond with his father.

kurgan.name: Kurgan
kurgan.summary: A type of burial mound built over a grave, originating on the Pontic–Caspian steppe and spreading through Central Asia and Europe, with the earliest examples dating to the fourth millennium BC.

alans.name: Alans
alans.summary: Ancient Iranian-speaking nomadic people who migrated to the North Caucasus and later parts of Europe and North Africa, related to the Sarmatians and first recorded by Roman sources in the 1st century CE.

andronovo-culture.name: Andronovo culture
andronovo-culture.summary: A group of related Late Bronze Age cultures from about 2000 to 1150 BCE, spanning from the southern Urals to central Siberia and western Xinjiang, generally agreed to have been Indo-Iranian.

ukok-plateau.name: Ukok Plateau
ukok-plateau.summary: A grassland plateau in the Altai Mountains of southwestern Siberia, part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site and habitat for snow leopards and other endangered species.

siberian-ice-maiden.name: Siberian Ice Maiden
siberian-ice-maiden.summary: Naturally preserved mummy of a young woman from the Pazyryk culture, discovered in 1993 on Siberia's Ukok Plateau, preserved by ice for about 2,400 years.

genghis-khan.name: Genghis Khan
genghis-khan.summary: Founder of the Mongol Empire (c. 1162-1227), who united the Mongol tribes and conquered large parts of China and Central Asia.

khirigsuur.name: Khirigsuur
khirigsuur.summary: A type of Bronze Age burial found in Mongolic-speaking regions, made of a central stone mound over a burial chamber with a surrounding stone enclosure and outer mounds, often linked to deer-stone monuments.

arzhan-culture.name: Arzhan culture
arzhan-culture.summary: An early Scythian culture of Saka burial mounds in Tuva, Russia, from the 8th to 7th century BC, considered the earliest known Scythian culture.

king-cheng-of-zhou.name: King Cheng of Zhou
king-cheng-of-zhou.summary: Second king of China's Zhou dynasty, who reigned roughly 1042 to 1021 BC under the regency of the Duke of Zhou during his minority.

guoyu-book.name: Guoyu (Discourses of the States)
guoyu-book.summary: An ancient Chinese text of 240 speeches attributed to rulers, spanning the Spring and Autumn period, compiled from the 5th to late 4th century BC by an unknown author.

chu-state.name: Chu
chu-state.summary: An ancient Chinese state of the Zhou dynasty, founded in the early 8th century BC south of the Zhou heartland, annexed by Qin in 223 BC.

berel-kurgan.name: Berel kurgan
berel-kurgan.summary: An archaeological site in eastern Kazakhstan with 5th- to 3rd-century BCE Saka burial mounds containing lavish gold jewelry and richly decorated horses.

warring-states-period.name: Warring States period
warring-states-period.summary: A Chinese era from about 475 to 221 BC marked by intense warfare and political consolidation, ending when the state of Qin conquered its rivals and founded the first imperial dynasty.

the-great-summons.name: The Great Summons
the-great-summons.summary: Ancient Chinese poem in the Chu ci anthology, attributed to Qu Yuan or Jing Cuo, from a shamanic tradition of summoning back the soul of someone who appeared to have died.

chu-ci.name: Chu Ci
chu-ci.summary: An ancient anthology of Chinese poetry mainly attributed to Qu Yuan and Song Yu, compiled in its traditional 17-section form by the 2nd-century librarian Wang Yi.
